lines.trans: There are moments when we are desperately angry at ourselves because of the deeds
Because of the people who are happy without us.
Because of the words we spoke without thinking.
Maybe it is time to stop hating ourselves and try to fix something?

Because of the people who are happy without us.
Because of the words we spoke without thinking.
Maybe it is time to stop hating ourselves and try to fix something?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you (informal)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You're greedy!
Have you got any more?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ступить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'acted', paired with 'поступать'.

examples.trans: Yulia needs to get into university.
He got into university.

examples.text: Вы плохо поступили, но хотя бы совесть есть.
examples.trans: You acted badly, but at least you have a conscience.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How was it in Hungary?
As you all know...
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'man' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У мужчины бывает не только жена.
examples.trans: A man can have more than just a wife.
This man is waiting for you.

examples.text: У мужчины, мальчик, бывает не только жена. Это моя девушка.
examples.trans: A man, my boy, can have more than just a wife. She's my girlfriend.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пасибо'). Common neuter noun meaning 'thank you' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Thanks, Dad!
Thank you for your trust!

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Thank you for your trust!
Thanks for the present.
What for?

meanings.note: Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'silence' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть молчание.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always silence.
The chef immediately noticed where the silence was.

meanings.en: to happen, to exist, there can be
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'occur, happen', paired with 'быть'.

examples.text: У мужчины бывает не только жена.
examples.trans: A man can have more than just a wife.
That happens.

examples.text: У мужчины, мальчик, бывает не только жена. Это моя девушка.
examples.trans: A man, my boy, can have more than just a wife. She's my girlfriend.

meanings.note: From Latin 'momentum' (movement, brief span of time).

examples.trans: At any moment.
One minute, one moment.

examples.text: А мне что-то уже не хочется. Момент упущен.
examples.trans: Somehow I don't feel like it anymore. The moment has passed.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'when', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: When I grow up, I'll be the mayor.
Oh yeah? When?

examples.text: Правда? Когда вы не ели мясо?
examples.trans: Really? When did you not eat meat?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'чаянно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: He desperately searched for a way out.
The cook desperately tried to save the situation.

meanings.en: to be angry, to get mad
meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'we get angry', paired with 'разозлиться'.

examples.text: А знаешь, почему ты так злишься?
examples.trans: And do you know why you are so angry?
Don't be angry with me, please.

examples.text: Хорошо. А знаешь, почему ты так злишься?
examples.trans: Fine. Do you know why you're so angry?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself (myself, yourself...)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'll do it myself.
He knows himself.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'themselves', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I feel good.
He only thinks about himself.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'because of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Из-за вашей Лёли весь класс зовёт меня врунишкой!
examples.trans: Because of your Lyolya the whole class calls me a little liar!
We were late because of the rain.

examples.text: А трава в мешках сгорела. Из-за вас!
examples.trans: And the herbs in the sacks burned. Because of you!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ступок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'actions / deeds' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I committed a very foolish act.

examples.text: Это был благородный и смелый поступок.
examples.trans: It was a noble and brave deed.

examples.text: Соколов, не делай сейчас таких глупых поступков.
examples.trans: Sokolov, do not do such foolish deeds right now.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'who', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This is a mayor who keeps his word.
Where is the book that was here?

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'овершить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'committed', paired with 'совершать'.

examples.trans: He made a mistake.
Daddy's already had his cold dip.
Rise and shine! Daddy's already had his cold dip.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'people' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He is a good person.
There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'частливый'). Qualitative adjective formed with the productive suffix '-тельный'/'-ливый'. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('happy').

examples.trans: I'm very happy.
The film has a happy ending.

examples.text: Ты сейчас один против всех. Счастливого конца не будет.
examples.trans: Right now you're alone against everyone. There won't be a happy ending.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'without', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's no problem.
This time there's no trick.
That's no problem at all.

meanings.note: Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common feminine noun meaning 'daughter' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Thank you, dear!
Their daughter goes to school.

examples.text: Мой Гриша мечтать об этом не мог! Спасибо, дочка!
examples.trans: My Grisha could not even dream of this! Thank you, dear!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
That's mine.
No. That's mine.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'again', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It's another trick.
Rain again.

examples.text: Нина, не слушай. Это опять обман.
examples.trans: Nina, don't listen. It's another trick.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'yes', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh yeah?
Yes, it's me.
Oh yeah? When?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'dad' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Hi, Dad!
Dad is at home.
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to me', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
I grew up here.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.
It's very hard.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: It smells bad here.
I feel bad.

examples.text: Послушайте, а можно в другое место? Здесь плохо пахнет.
examples.trans: Listen, could we go somewhere else? It smells bad in here.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лово'). Common neuter noun meaning 'words' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: But you gave your word!
He keeps his word.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'told', paired with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: What did you say?
Excuse me, where's the metro?
Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.en: to think it over, to give it a thought
meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'умать').

examples.trans: I'll think about it.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.
I've been thinking.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'maybe', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Maybe you could help?
Maybe tomorrow.
I thought maybe you wouldn't see me.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'it's time', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Time to go home.
It's time for us to go.
All right, Arkashenka. We'll be off, it's time.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'стать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to stop', paired with 'переставать'.

examples.text: Да перестаньте! Я двадцать лет в карты не играла.
examples.trans: Oh, stop it! I haven't played cards for twenty years.
The rain finally stopped.

examples.text: Иначе я перестану давать тебе деньги!
examples.trans: Otherwise I'll stop giving you money!

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'навидеть'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to hate', paired with 'возненавидеть'.

examples.trans: Why do you hate me?
I hate Mondays.

examples.text: Скажи мне в глаза. За что ты меня так ненавидишь?
examples.trans: Say it to my face. Why do you hate me so much?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'пытаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to try / attempt'.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и попытаться вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and to try on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют попытаться.
examples.trans: In our kitchen everyone knows how to to try.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'something; somehow', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Has something happened?
Somehow I'm tired.
I can't see it somehow.

meanings.en: to fix, to correct, to put right
meanings.note: Prefix 'ис-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'править'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to fix / make right', paired with 'исправлять'.

examples.trans: Excuse us, we will fix everything.

examples.text: Ученик быстро исправил ошибку в тетради.
examples.trans: The pupil quickly corrected the mistake in his notebook.

examples.text: Да, вы знаете, это очень серьёзная операция. Мы всё исправим. До свидания!
examples.trans: Yes, you know, it is a very serious operation. We'll fix everything. Goodbye!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'at least', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Хочу хотя бы один спокойный день!
examples.trans: I want at least one calm day!
Then you will have at least tried.

examples.text: Пожалуйста, выслушайте меня хотя бы минуту.
examples.trans: Please, listen to me for at least a minute.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'would', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I would think about it.
I'd buy a house.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.
